title: Nokoss
author: Aïssatou Mbaye
desc: The pounded base nearly every Senegalese dish starts from — onion, garlic, nététou, chilli and pepper, used a third at a time.
longDesc: If rof is what goes inside the fish, nokoss is what goes into the pot. One onion, two cloves of garlic, a handful of nététou, two bird's eye chillies, half a bell pepper, an optional bouillon cube and salt, pounded or chopped together. Its distinguishing feature against every other West African pepper base is the nététou — fermented locust bean — which brings the savoury depth that tomato and onion alone cannot. Senegalese cooks add it in stages rather than all at once: a third with the browning meat, a third into the water, the last third near the end.
ingredients: // A second documented formula, from the same author's thiébou yap
// 1 onion, 1/2 bell pepper, 1 tsp pepper, 8 cloves garlic and salt
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a blender
steps: Pound or chop the onion, garlic, nététou, chillies and bell pepper together with the salt and the optional bouillon cube.
// Use it in thirds, not all at once:
Add a third with the meat or fish as it browns.
Add a third to the water once the pot comes to the boil.
Add the last third near the end, then taste and adjust the salt.
chefTips: The nététou is what makes this Senegalese rather than generically West African. Without it you have a pepper base; with it you have nokoss.
In thirds, by the author's own method. One third with the browning, one third into the broth, one third at the end — it layers rather than flattening into one note.
Pounded, not blended smooth, if you have a mortar. The texture carries through into the finished broth.
Taste and re-salt after the last third goes in. Nététou is salty and variable, so seasoning at the start is guesswork.
Her other documented formula uses eight cloves of garlic and a teaspoon of pepper with no nététou listed — a much more garlic-forward base. Both are hers and both work.
Make it fresh. It is ten minutes of work and it does not keep as well as a dried spice mix.
Note this is a different preparation from nokos, the dry spice blend published in a Senegalese chef's fonio book, despite the near-identical name.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the nététou, which is the point of it.
Adding it all at once at the start.
Blending it to a smooth purée.
Salting fully before the last third goes in.
Confusing it with the dry nokos spice blend.
sources: Adapted from the nokoss component of 'Ceeb bu weex, thièb bou wekh ou thieboudiene blanc', aistoucuisine.com. BYLINE: Aïssatou Mbaye. Date: 9 mai 2016. TWO-PASS.
Ingredients as printed in French: '1 oignon'; '2 gousses d'ail'; 'une poignée de nététou'; '2 piments oiseau'; '1/2 poivron'; 'un bouillon cube (si vous souhaitez)'; 'du sel'.

A SECOND FORMULA BY THE SAME AUTHOR, recorded unreconciled, from 'Thiébou Yap avec le riz basmati de la vallée du Sénégal' (31 octobre 2017): one onion, half a bell pepper, '1 cuillère à café de poivre', '8 gousses d'ail' and salt — no nététou named, and eight cloves of garlic against the other version's two. Both are printed by the same cook. Neither is corrected toward the other.

THE STAGED APPLICATION is from the same 2017 recipe, which prints '1/3 du nokoss' with the browning meat, a further third into the water, and the remainder added near the end with a re-tasting of the broth.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE ENTRY: nokoss is called for by name across the Senegalese rice dishes, stews and soups in this collection. It is a real standing preparation in Senegalese kitchens, not an ingredient list fragment.

ON THE NÉTÉTOU: fermented locust bean, Parkia biglobosa, also called soumbala and equivalent to Nigerian iru and Ghanaian dawadawa. Its from-scratch fermentation is published at SEN087 with an observable endpoint (borrowed from Nigerian and Burkinabè studies, as that entry states). Guedj and yeet, the other two Senegalese fermented seasonings, are published at SEN088 and SEN089 as documented processes with a finished-product description and no in-process doneness test.
NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH NOKOS, a dry spice blend published by Pierre Thiam in 'The Fonio Cookbook' and recorded separately at SEN091. The names are nearly identical and the preparations are not.
NO YIELD is printed. The ten servings above is editorial.
storage: 2 days refrigerated, or freeze in portions. Best fresh.
reheating: Not applicable — added to the pot raw.
healthBenefits: Nététou is high in plant protein and B vitamins, and its alkaline fermentation improves amino-acid availability.
Garlic and onion supply organosulfur compounds and quercetin.
Capsaicin from the bird's eye chillies.
Replaces much of the salt and bouillon a dish would otherwise need.
culturalNote: Every West African cuisine has its aromatic base and the differences between them are the differences between the cuisines — Nigerian obe ata leans on tomato and pepper, Ghanaian chalé sauce on blended raw tomato, and Senegalese nokoss on fermented locust bean. Senegalese cooks add it in thirds, which is a technique rather than a recipe.
